newsitem.title: USA: Stocks lower, bonds eke gains before jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Stocks lower, bonds eke gains before jobs data.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks drifted lower and bonds edged higher Thursday as investors turned cautious ahead of Friday's September payrolls report.
The dollar eked out a fresh 10-week high against the German mark before a mild retreat against major currencies.

"Stocks and bonds are waiting to see the employment report and that will set the tone for stocks for the next three weeks, along with earnings reports. Today, people are just positioning themselves," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.
After surging 65 points over the past four trading days, the Dow Jones industrial average slipped 1.12 points to 5,932.85. The blue-chip index set back-to-back records on Tuesday and Wednesday.
In the broader market, declining issues outpaced advances by 1,231 to 1,106 with 386 million shares traded on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks fell 1.23 to 692.78 after scoring its third consecutive record finish on Wednesday.
The NYSE Composite index was off 0.40 at 370.14 after snaring its fifth straight record on Wednesday. The average price per share fell 4 cents.
The technology-rich Nasdaq Composite index slipped 3.02 to 1,233.09 after rallying 15 points on Wednesday.
The key 30-year Treasury bond edged up 1/32, leaving the yield unchanged at 6.84 percent -- the lowest since Aug. 22.
Both stock and bond markets barely reacted to economic data out Thursday, focusing instead on Friday's jobs report.
Economists expect September payrolls to rise 166,000, a considerably tamer rate of growth than August's 250,000 increase and the more than 200,000 each month since May.
"We are not expecting a surprise and any surprise would hit the market hard," said Harry Laubscher of Tucker Anthony.
"We are well into overbought territory. But fund managers are quite bullish and optimistic about tomorrow's report ...," said Laubscher, a market analyst.
The dollar reached 1.5341 marks in Europe but slipped to 1.5310 marks in late trading vs. 1.5325 late Wednesday.
The dollar fetched 111.47 Japanese yen, down from a high of 111.97 yen in Tokyo and 111.87 yen late Wednesday.

A 10-year low in warehouse supplies lifted coffee at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange to a four-week high. December coffee futures rose 2.05 cents to 107.45 cents after peaking earlier at 107.70.
Heating oil rose to the highest level since the Gulf War as the onset of cool autumn weather exacerbated fears of supply shortages this winter.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, November heating oil settled 2.71 cents higher at 74.69 cents. November crude oil was up 0.76 cent at $24.81 per barrel and November gasoline was up 1.26 cents at 63.68 cents per gallon.

Cattle prices tumbled as traders believed recent gains in cash markets have run their course and prices will move lower. At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, December live cattle closed down the 1.50-cent-per-pound daily limit at 66.300 cents.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index hit a record 4,024.3 points before closing down 15.1 points at 4,000 points. In Tokyo, the 225-issue Nikkei average ended down 167.10 points, or 0.78, percent at 21,331.50.
